questions.question_text: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=5\ln x$ at the point $(1,0)$.

options.why: Used $(0,0)$ instead of $(1,0)$ when substituting into $y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1})$.
Found the normal instead of the tangent by taking the negative reciprocal of the gradient.
Used the gradient of $y=\ln x$ and ignored the coefficient $5$.

questions.question_text:
The tangent to $y=\ln x$ has gradient $\dfrac{1}{7}$ at the point $P$.
Find the coordinates of $P$.

options.why: Read $\dfrac{1}{x}=\dfrac{1}{7}$ as $x=\dfrac{1}{7}$, taking the reciprocal one time too many.
Found $x=7$ correctly but wrote the $y$-coordinate as $7$ instead of evaluating $\ln 7$.
Swapped the $x$- and $y$-coordinates of the point.

questions.question_text:
The proof of $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\ln x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$ differentiates both sides of $e^{\ln x}=x$.
Writing $u'(x)$ for the derivative of $\ln x$, the chain rule gives $u'(x)e^{\ln x}$ for the left-hand side and $1$ for the right-hand side.
Which line completes the proof?

options.why: Replaced $e^{\ln x}$ with $e^{x}$, but the identity says $e^{\ln x}=x$.
Added the two factors instead of keeping the product the chain rule produces.
Differentiated the right-hand side $x$ as $x$ rather than as $1$.

questions.question_text: Find the value of $x>0$ for which the derivative of $y=2x^{2}-36\ln x$ is zero.

options.why: Ignored the $x$ in the denominator and solved $4x=36$ instead of $4x=\dfrac{36}{x}$.
Solved $4x^{2}=36$ as $x^{2}=36$, dropping the coefficient $4$.
Wrote the derivative of $36\ln x$ as $\dfrac{1}{36x}$, giving $4x=\dfrac{1}{36x}$.

questions.question_text: Find the $y$-intercept of the tangent to $y=\ln x$ at the point where $x=e^{2}$.

options.why: Gave the $y$-coordinate of the point of contact instead of the intercept of the tangent.
Subtracted the wrong way round, computing $\dfrac{1}{e^{2}}\times e^{2}-2$ instead of $2-\dfrac{1}{e^{2}}\times e^{2}$.
Used a gradient of $1$ instead of $\dfrac{1}{e^{2}}$ when substituting $x=0$.
Differentiated $10\ln x$ to $0$, treating the logarithm term as a constant.
Differentiated $10\ln x$ correctly but dropped the derivative of $-2x$.
Treated $\ln x$ as $x^{-1}$ and used $\dfrac{10}{x^{2}}$ for the derivative of $10\ln x$.
